title: Workforce and forecasting
summary: Forecast views, creation methods, the editor, and the short-term weeks that are allowed to build a schedule.

lessons.title: A forecast is a WFM plan for interactions, not a routing method
lessons.summary: Workforce management is one WEM product. The forecast article names the metrics and the permissions.
paras: The WEM article is the family: recording, quality, speech and text analytics, and workforce management. The forecast article is narrower. Forecasts help you plan how many interactions to expect. The metrics it names are pattern, volume as interactions offered, and average handle time made of average talk time, average hold time, and average after call work. That handle time is not the conversation-score priority on a queue.

The forecast article lists these permissions: Workforce Management > Forecast – Add, Delete, Edit, and View; Analytics > conversationsAggregate – View; and Analytics > taskmanagementAggregate – View. The WFM track in this lab covers business units, schedules, adherence, and time off. This chapter stays on the forecast pages: views, creation methods, the editor, and what is allowed to generate a schedule.

lessons.title: Short-term weeks can schedule. Long-term weeks cannot
lessons.summary: Six weeks of intervals on one side. Up to two years of days and weeks on the other.
paras: The forecast article describes two views. The short-term view is interval-level data, one week at a time, for up to six weeks depending on the forecast length, and it can generate schedules. The long-term view is day- and week-level data, up to one year at a time and up to two years total, for seasonality and trends. It cannot generate schedules. Schedules use only the short-term component, whose maximum is six weeks, so a longer horizon needs multiple forecasts.

The forecasts list shows up to 26 weeks before and 26 weeks after the earlier of the current week or the last week that has a forecast. Search finds forecasts outside that window, including a start date up to 104 weeks in the future. You do not have to pick the exact start week. Available for Schedule is the checkbox that lets the forecast appear when you generate a schedule. The default time zone is the business unit’s, and an administrator can change the displayed zone.

lessons.title: Four creation methods, and a 130-week outer limit
lessons.summary: Automatic best method, weighted history, imported source days, or a finished short-term file.
paras: The add-a-forecast article lets you pick a start week up to 26 weeks in the past or 104 weeks in the future. The end date cannot pass 130 weeks from the start week. If you type a longer duration, Genesys Cloud reduces it and shows a message. Creation methods on that page are Automatic best method selection, Weighted Historical Index, Weighted Historical Index with Source Data Import, and Import Short-Term Interval Forecast Data.

Automatic best method uses the available historical data, with outlier detection and fixes for missing data. Weighted historical index with source data import uses a CSV instead of system history and allows up to eight source days, such as eight historical Mondays for the forecast Monday. Import Short-Term Interval Forecast Data brings a finished file of at most six weeks, and every row must fall inside the forecast duration or the system returns an error. For Genesys Cloud EX data that is injected from outside, the article says to use Automatic best method: weighted historical index caches conversation data older than one day and permanently excludes data that was not injected yet.

lessons.title: The editor shows history as read-only lines
lessons.summary: Short-term granularity is 15, 30, or 60 minutes. Long-term granularity is daily or weekly.
paras: The forecast editor article puts Short-Term Forecast and Long-Term Forecast on two icons. Short-term granularity choices are 15 minutes, 30 minutes, and 60 minutes. Long-term choices are daily and weekly. Pointing at the graph shows the data for that time. The lines are the historic data used to create the forecast, and they are read-only. Colors match the metrics.

The editor sits below the graph. Dragging selects a smaller date range, and clicking outside the selection clears that zoom. Checkboxes on the left change which metric variables are included. This page does not say that editing a line rewrites history. If you need to change the forecast itself, use the modification controls on the forecast article rather than assuming the historic line is editable.

lessons.title: The schedule has to sit inside the short-term weeks
lessons.summary: Generation offers a forecast only when those weeks cover the schedule, and only one schedule is generated at a time.
paras: The schedules article lists three generation choices: create a schedule with a forecast, create one without a forecast, and create a blank schedule. A forecast-based schedule has to use a forecast marked Available for Schedule, and the schedule’s dates have to fall inside that forecast’s short-term weeks. The article’s example: a six-week schedule must align with those six short-term weeks, and a four-week schedule must fall inside a four-, five-, or six-week short-term portion. The generate dialog’s maximum number of weeks is 6.

The generate-from-forecast article says you can generate only one schedule per business unit at a time. The new attempt shows in Last Scheduling Attempts. A schedule without a forecast is a blank pattern of shifts when no forecast exists. It is not a secret use of the long-term view. The forecast article adds the planning rule in front of all of this: if two business units share load, someone has to adjust the forecast by hand, because the product expects a clean split of resources and work.

lessons.title: Use the forecast, then go back to the floor
lessons.summary: Intraday compares the plan with what happened. Adherence is a different WFM page.
paras: The workforce management overview lists developing forecasts and comparing the intraday forecast with actual values, next to blank schedules, forecast-based schedules, and schedules without a forecast. The comparison is how you notice that Tuesday’s interval was wrong. It does not rewrite the historic line in the editor, and it does not change who ACD offers.

Adherence, time off, and the business-unit structure stay on the WFM track. Quality forms and speech programs stay on the quality chapter. A forecast that cannot explain an abandon rate is not a broken bullseye ring. Say which system you are looking at before you change a skill, a ring, or a schedule.
